profile.descriptor: Community Program Coordinator, Archival Researcher & Field Workshop Facilitator
profile.introduction: I organize neighborhood learning initiatives, document local history, and design practical guides that help people share tools, stories, and outdoor spaces. (Sample profile for the SareyBothPortfolio template.)
biography: Over the past several years, my work has centered on practical ways neighbors can learn from one another—whether through a lending cabinet of heirloom seeds, an oral history booth at the weekend market, or an illustrated repair handbook.

I enjoy bridging careful research with welcoming, hands-on gatherings. When a topic feels intimidating at first, a clear worksheet, a patient conversation, and a shared table usually make it approachable.
Outside of organized programs, I spend my mornings walking local creek trails with a pocket sketchbook, binding small linen notebooks, and testing seasonal preservation recipes.

highlights.title: Neighborhood Seed Library & Seasonal Growing Guide
highlights.summary: Co-created a self-serve wooden seed cabinet and color-coded planting cards Hosted at three branch libraries.
highlights.roleOrContribution: Program co-organizer, planting card writer, and volunteer coordinator
highlights.context: Local gardeners wanted a simple way to exchange regionally adapted vegetable and native pollinator seeds without requiring membership fees or complex check-out software.
outcomes: Installed weather-tight seed cabinets across three neighborhood library branches.
Published a 24-card bilingual seasonal planting index for first-time balcony and yard growers.
Coordinated 14 recurring volunteers for autumn seed-cleaning and envelope-packing sessions.

coverImage.alt: Neighborhood Seed Library wooden cabinet and labeled packets

gallery.alt: Color-coded seed catalog cards organized by growing season
gallery.caption: Three-tier difficulty cards help visitors pick varieties suited to pots, raised beds, or shaded patios.

gallery.alt: Seed sorting workshop table with glass jars and paper envelopes
gallery.caption: Monthly sorting tables bring together experienced savers and curious neighbors.

body.text: Starting with a Single Repurposed Card Catalog

The idea began when a retired librarian offered an unused 15-drawer oak index cabinet. Rather than tracking individual borrowers, we designed the cabinet around trust and clarity: anyone could take up to five packets in the spring and return harvested seeds in labeled envelopes at the end of the season.
How We Structured the Reference Cards

Early feedback showed that newcomers felt unsure about which seeds could thrive in small containers versus open garden beds. We grouped the drawers into three clear categories and printed durable divider cards with sowing depth, sun needs, and harvest notes.

items: Green stripe: Easy container and windowsill varieties (lettuce, bush beans, radishes, calendula).
Terracotta stripe: Mid-season garden staples with straightforward seed saving (tomatoes, peas, peppers).
Slate stripe: Biennial crops and native perennials requiring cross-pollination awareness.

body.text: Having a five-sentence card right inside the drawer took away all the guesswork for my first balcony planter box.

body.alt: Color-coded seed catalog cards organized by growing season
body.caption: Divider cards use both color bands and clear typography for quick browsing.

highlights.title: Riverfront Oral History Listening Archive
highlights.summary: Recorded, transcribed, and indexed 28 conversational interviews with longtime riverfront residents and dock workers.
highlights.roleOrContribution: Lead interviewer, audio archivist, and exhibition co-curator
highlights.context: As former industrial riverfront blocks transitioned into public parks, the local historical society wanted to preserve firsthand memories of everyday life along the working waterfront.
outcomes: Collected 28 full-length audio interviews with signed public-archive release forms.
Created time-stamped transcripts and a subject index covering 1955 through 2010.
Set up a two-headphone listening station at the community center's autumn heritage week.

coverImage.alt: Audio waveform and archival index cards for the Riverfront Oral History project

gallery.alt: Portable recording setup with two microphones and interview prompt cards
gallery.caption: A compact two-microphone kit allowed us to record in kitchens, boat sheds, and library study rooms.

body.text: Designing Unhurried Conversations

Rather than arriving with a rigid questionnaire, we mailed participants a postcard of historic riverfront maps a week before each session. Holding a physical map sparked immediate, specific stories about ferry crossings, seasonal floods, and neighborhood bakeries.
Archival Workflow

items: Pre-interview coffee chat to explain consent options and review old photographs.
Uncompressed WAV recording using dual cardioid microphones in quiet home settings.
Full human-reviewed transcript paired with a 3-minute thematic audio excerpt.
Deposit of archival master files and printed transcripts with the county library.

highlights.title: Accessible Creek Trail Pocket Guide
highlights.summary: Surveyed five local watershed paths to document surface types, slope grades, seating intervals, and transit stops.
highlights.roleOrContribution: Field surveyor, cartographic illustrator, and layout editor
highlights.context: Standard park maps listed trail mileage but omitted practical accessibility details needed by stroller users, mobility-aid users, and walkers seeking frequent rest benches.
outcomes: Measured surface width, cross-slope, and bench spacing across 11.5 miles of urban trails.
Produced a foldable print brochure and screen-reader-friendly web table.
Distributed 600 copies through senior centers, physical therapy clinics, and trailhead kiosks.

coverImage.alt: Topographic map and trail accessibility markers

gallery.alt: Trail grade and rest bench interval diagram
gallery.caption: Elevation profiles call out exact distances between shaded benches and paved pull-outs.

body.text: Measuring What Actually Matters on the Ground

Working alongside four neighborhood volunteers with different mobility devices, we walked each trail segment with a measuring wheel, digital level, and notebook. Instead of labeling a path simply 'easy' or 'moderate,' we recorded concrete observations so visitors could decide for themselves.

items: Surface composition: compacted crushed granite, boardwalk planks, or smooth asphalt.
Exact distance in feet between benches with backrests.
Curb-cut alignment at the nearest bus stop and parking area.

highlights.title: Weekend Repair Cafe Volunteer Handbook
highlights.summary: Compiled a practical intake and safety manual for a monthly pop-up event fixing small appliances, bicycles, and garments.
highlights.roleOrContribution: Handbook author and intake desk coordinator
highlights.context: Our monthly repair gathering grew from five fixers to twenty, creating a need for consistent safety checks, spare-part checklists, and friendly visitor expectations.
outcomes: Standardized electrical safety checklists and clear house rules for collaborative repair.
Reduced visitor wait-time confusion by introducing a simple visual triage board.
Shared the handbook under an open license for three neighboring town chapters.

coverImage.alt: Illustrated handbook and hand tools for community repair cafe

body.text: Turning Repair into a Shared Learning Moment

The goal of a community repair table isn't drop-off servicing—it's sitting beside a neighbor to open a toaster or mend a jacket seam together. The handbook gives volunteers simple prompts to explain diagnostic steps clearly and safely.

highlights.title: Seasonal Preservation & Fermentation Study Group
highlights.summary: Documented a year-long personal learning milestone testing small-batch vegetable fermentation and salt-ratio logs.
highlights.roleOrContribution: Independent learner and study-group note keeper
highlights.context: Set a personal goal to learn traditional lacto-fermentation methods across four seasons using surplus produce from the neighborhood farm stand.
outcomes: Logged 36 small-batch trials with precise weight, brine percentage, and ambient temperature notes.
Hosted a casual autumn tasting and recipe swap for twelve neighbors.
Bound a hand-stitched kitchen reference booklet of reliable ratios.

coverImage.alt: Seasonal preservation jars and handwritten tasting log

body.text: Keeping a Repeatable Kitchen Log
By tracking gram weights, salt percentages by total weight, and kitchen shelf temperatures, even unexpected textures became useful data points for the next batch.

articles.title: How We Set Up a Self-Serve Neighborhood Seed Cabinet
articles.summary: Practical lessons on drawer labels, moisture control, and seasonal volunteer rhythms from our first two years.

coverImage.alt: Neighborhood Seed Library wooden cabinet and labeled packets

body.text: Keep the Check-Out Process Frictionless

When we visited other lending libraries before launching ours, the single biggest bottleneck was complicated sign-out sheets. We replaced paper ledgers with a simple tally counter and pre-stamped coin envelopes.
Three Supplies That Make a Difference

items: Number 3 kraft coin envelopes with a pre-printed stamp for variety name, year, and neighborhood.
Silica gel packets tucked into the back of each wooden drawer to keep humidity steady.
A small clipboard for visitors to request varieties they hope to see next spring.

body.text: Start with ten reliable varieties that grow well on a sunny porch, and let neighbors shape the collection from there.

articles.title: Preparing for a Calm Kitchen-Table Oral History Interview
articles.summary: A checklist for testing microphones, choosing visual prompts, and helping narrators feel at ease.

coverImage.alt: Portable recording setup with two microphones and interview prompt cards

body.text: Room Acoustics at the Kitchen Table

Hard table surfaces bounce sound right back into tabletop microphones. Laying a folded woven tablecloth or wool scarf beneath the mic stands immediately softens reflections and removes the clatter of teacups.

items: Arrive fifteen minutes early so equipment setup finishes before the conversation begins.
Check refrigerator and window fan noise with headphones before pressing record.
Record thirty seconds of room tone at the end of the session to help with editing.

articles.title: Designing Pocket Field Guides That Survive a Rainy Walk
articles.summary: Typography, paper weight, and folding patterns that stay legible when carried in a coat pocket.

coverImage.alt: Topographic map and trail accessibility markers

body.text: Why Accordion Folds Beat Multi-Page Booklets Outdoors

On a breezy trail, flipping through stapled pages with one hand while holding an umbrella or mobility cane is frustrating. A six-panel accordion fold lets walkers refold the map to the exact segment they are currently traversing.
